The parabola is the set of all points in a plane equidistant from a fixed point called the focus and a fixed line called the directrix. As a conic section with an eccentricity of exactly one, it represents the critical boundary between the closed ellipse and the open hyperbola. Parabolas are of immense practical importance in science and engineering, defining the trajectories of projectiles under uniform gravity and the reflective properties of antennas, telescopes, and headlights. The mathematical study of the parabola dates back to classical antiquity, where Archimedes's quadrature of the parabola served as a major precursor to calculus. In vertex form, a parabola is expressed as y equals a times x minus h squared plus k, where h and k is the vertex. In focus-directrix form, it's x minus h squared equals four p times y minus k for a vertically opening parabola, where p is the distance from the vertex to the focus and also from the vertex to the directrix. The latus rectum is the chord passing through the focus and parallel to the directrix. Its length is four p, and its endpoints lie on the parabola. The eccentricity equals exactly one, placing it as the mathematical limit between the ellipse with eccentricity less than one and the hyperbola with eccentricity greater than one. The parabola has a remarkable optical and acoustical reflection property. Any light or sound ray traveling parallel to the axis of symmetry reflects off the parabolic surface directly into the focus. A parabola can also be generated as the envelope of a family of circles whose centers lie on a line and which all pass through a fixed point. In physics, the path of a projectile launched under uniform gravity is a parabola—Galileo demonstrated this. Archimedes proved in his work The Quadrature of the Parabola that the area enclosed by a parabola and a line equals four-thirds times the area of an inscribed triangle, utilizing a geometric infinite series that prefigured calculus. The cables of a suspension bridge with a uniformly distributed load along its horizontal deck hang in a parabolic curve, which is distinct from the catenary curve of a free-hanging chain. The parabola is a fundamental bridge between algebra and geometry, representing the graph of every quadratic equation and the physical path of falling objects. In optics and acoustics, its reflective properties focus energy—gathering faint light from distant stars in reflecting telescopes or projecting a beam from car headlights.
